content: The number of specialist nurses dedicated to the care and management of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has been increasing. However, there is limited evidence to date that demonstrates the effectiveness of these specialist nursing interventions. This review was conducted to evaluate the impact of such interventions on the management of IBD, including access to treatment, disease remission, morbidity, and quality of life. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was performed across databases such as the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and the British Nursing Index. References from related papers were also reviewed, and hand searches of gastroenterology conference proceedings were conducted. The last search was completed on September 30, 2008. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series studies that focused on interventions by gastroenterology and IBD specialist nurses. These studies aimed to improve access to care and outcomes for patients with ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two investigators. Any disagreements were resolved through consensus. Only one randomized controlled trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 100 IBD patients who were randomly assigned to receive either a specialist nurse-delivered counseling package (n = 50) or routine outpatient clinic follow-up (n = 50). Assessments were conducted at baseline, six months, and 12 months. The included study was of low methodological quality. It did not report data on several important outcomes, including disease remission, patient compliance, clinical improvement, utilization of nurse-led services, patient satisfaction, hospital admissions, outpatient attendance, progression to surgery, length of hospital stay, or cost-effectiveness. The study did report pooled mean mental health scores at six months, which were higher in patients who received nurse-led counseling compared to those who received routine follow-up. However, this difference was not statistically significant (weighted mean difference [WMD] 3.67; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.44 to 7.77; P = 0.08). Other pooled assessments of physical and psychological well-being also showed no statistically significant differences between the two groups. The authors concluded that while specialist nurse counseling interventions may offer some benefits for IBD patients, the evidence from the single included study is of low quality. Therefore, the results should be interpreted with caution. Higher-quality trials are needed to better assess the impact of specialist nursing interventions on the care and management of patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
